THESE FOUR ARE BUILT AND RUNNING.

Every token, padding, radius and font size is lifted from src/enlightenment/ui/index.html. Every plot is generated by the product's own plots.py, so the shapes here are the shapes the application draws.

They are the fidelity baseline and the component vocabulary. The five screens on page two extend it.

OPEN QUESTION A - your call, and it shapes the highest-value screen.

The expert-cue box needs to say "attention, but not an alarm". Red is alert, green is nominal, Blue 2 is structure, and copper-amber is excluded from product UI by house rule - so nothing in the palette is free for it.

The Reveal artboard has a tweak above it: ink-outline (implemented) or copper-amber (the house-rule exception). Flip it and pick one.

PALETTE RULES, MEASURED, AND TESTS ENFORCE THEM.

Blue 1 #385FAF is 2.45:1 on navy. It fails the text floor AND the 3:1 graphic floor, so it is fill and border only - never text, never status.

Alert red is #E06C69 (4.66:1) wherever it carries text. #C0504D (3.21:1) is large fills only.

Status is never colour alone: every one carries a glyph and a word.

OPEN QUESTION E - the first run.

Ninety seconds, zero prior knowledge, ending in one correct unaided call. The definition of done requires an operator who does not know what an element set is to reach a correct classification in under fifteen minutes, and this screen carries most of that.

Shown here at step 1 of 4. Pacing and scaffolding are the whole design. Is four steps right?

OPEN QUESTION B - progressive density.

The drill strips to almost nothing; this screen is full operational density. Same palette, same components, deliberately different information load - cognitive load theory says a novice on a dense display attends to the display, and the expertise-reversal effect says the scaffolds that fix that harm an expert.

How does an operator move between the two without it feeling like two tools?

OPEN QUESTION C - the hardest information-design problem in the product.

Two lanes on ONE shared clock, rather than two charts: the question is "when did the expert know, and when did I", and that is a comparison along one axis. Two charts make the reader do the alignment in their head, which is the work this screen exists to remove.

The self-explanation the operator wrote sits at the top and is quoted back. It precedes the reveal, is never scored, and is never reported.

OPEN QUESTION D - making "unscored" visible.

Operators need somewhere to be wrong in private or they will not explore. The sandbox has to feel safe at a glance without a childish treatment: a persistent pill and one plain sentence, no rating, no points, no scoring chrome anywhere on the screen.

Is that enough, or does it need to look more different from the drill?

THE PRIVACY DESIGN, WHICH IS NOT A LEGAL FOOTNOTE.

Supervisors see individual results - the owner's decision. Self-Determination Theory evidence says perceived surveillance erodes intrinsic motivation, which is the engine this product runs on, so the controls are part of the design.

What the operator is told, in the SAME WORDS the supervisor sees, is on the artboard. So is what is never shown: individual answers, miss rate, sandbox activity, self-explanations. A drill miss is the mechanism by which the product works.
